An undated LAUNCH temp-to-hire posting (Suffolk VA, search snippet, https://launchtws.com/jobs/13171/A-+Level+Diesel+Mechanic-Suffolk-Virginia) lists maximum pay of $26 for an A tech and $24 for a B tech with conversion at the same rate or higher. At a typical 1.4-1.5x that implies roughly $34-39 bill for experienced techs (A), against $52 for a 6-week trainee paid $27. LAUNCH bought the unit from TrueBlue (reason unknown). The refined lists LAUNCH as a competitor but never confronts its price and wage level. The two-week test also discriminates poorly: non-binding order forms with no deposit, pass at 5 of 40, and a wide 'reprice and rerun' band.

WIOA ON-THE-JOB-TRAINING SUBSIDY IS LIKELY INELIGIBLE FOR THIS STRUCTURE. The upside cost per graduate of $6,500 or less leans on WIOA OJT reimbursement. Iowa's policy (read this session, https://epolicy.iwd.iowa.gov/Policy/Index?id=146) says OJT may not be written with staffing agencies for positions that will be 'hired out'. Nebraska, Oakland and one Ohio board say the same or similar (search snippets). The one OJT source the refined cites (Wisconsin, read this session) is a superseded 2024 policy page that says nothing either way. Some boards allow agencies that provide regular ongoing work, but a 2-week-minimum temporary placement is what they exclude. Texas and Georgia board policies were not found. The direct beneficiary of OJT is the shop that hires directly, which strengthens the substitute.

RETENTION LEVERS ARE LEGALLY CONSTRAINED AND BOTH SIDES CAN CUT OUT THE BENCH. Hire-train-deploy firms usually lock trainees in with repayment or minimum-hours clauses. The DOL sued Smoothstack in July 2024 over such clauses (staffingindustry.com summary). California AB 692 (contracts from Jan 1, 2026) and New York's Trapped at Work Act (effective Dec 19, 2025) restrict them (law-firm alerts, search snippets). The refined offers only 'retention bonus, ladder, WIOA; unproven'. At a 93% markup a shop and a trained worker both gain by going direct. Trainees are also poachable by Torque ($23-26 plus a $2,000 retention bonus), Love's, Penske and Rush.

THE ENTERPRISE SEGMENT HAS NO EVIDENCE OF BUYING. 25 enterprise accounts at 24 FTE each is about 600 of 1,060 FTE (57%), about $59M of the $100M. These are dealer groups, lessors, roll-ups and large private fleets. The refined itself says Ryder and Penske insource, Amerit's academy is employees-only, and consolidators may build academies. Navistar ran a paid 12-month dealer apprenticeship (2021 snippet) and OEM-college pipelines exist. No named prospect, LOI or enterprise sales-cycle data. CAC per mid and small account is never recomputed under the new structure.

THE GROWTH-PACE ANALOG IS SLOW. Tradesmen International, the only scale analog cited, was established in 1992 (its own history page, search snippet). The earliest confirmation I found of it above $100M is its 2021 SIA listing, so roughly 28 years or fewer, not 7. The year-end FTE path (25, 90, 220, 420, 650, 850, 1,000) is faster than any precedent in the file, including Coltrain's 100 team members in a year (insiders with capital). Recruiting about 1,060 enrollees a year is about 10% of national trade-school output by the refined's own count.

LIABILITY AND COST STACK STILL UNPRICED. Workers' comp for brake and tire work, GL and staffing E&O, OSHA 1910.177 rim and tire exposure for 6-week trainees, and the 30-day free-replacement guarantee are unquoted. The model assumes 92% billed hours for a cohort-fed bench, optimistic when cohorts of 24 graduate on a schedule and demand arrives account by account. A burden of 1.30 is plausible only in low-comp states (unchecked).

PIVOT, NOT REFINEMENT. The business the critics called fatal (hourly yard crews sold to fleets) is abandoned. The replacement is a 5-12% EBITDA staffing company with a thin moat and, by the author's account, a likely end state of being acquired. Even at $100M, median unit economics give about $7M EBITDA on $15-30M of invested capital (A). The headline 'median $20M' is conditional on clearing the 90-day gates; the author says the unconditional median is a failed pilot, so the reported median overstates the typical outcome.
riskiest_assumption: Independent shops, dealers and private-fleet shops with open Level-1 work will pay a staffing-style bill rate of at least $50 an hour (about 1.85x the Level-1 wage; a 93% markup against a 35-45% skilled-trades staffing norm) for pre-trained Level-1s with a conversion option, instead of hiring direct at $24-28. Breakeven is about $47.50 an hour. I searched and found no evidence that shops or fleets buy temporary technicians at scale.
two_week_test: Cost under $500, one person, one metro. (1) Write a one-page offer: pre-trained Level-1 at $52 an hour, two-week minimum, 30-day replacement, $7,000 conversion after 520 hours, start in 4-6 weeks, with a non-binding order form that says plainly cohorts are not yet running. (2) Contact 40 targets: 15 independent heavy-duty shops, 10 dealer service managers, 10 private-fleet maintenance managers, 5 tire dealers with commercial service. Ask for open Level-1 requisitions and age, work turned away last month, current all-in cost of a direct hire, and a signed order form. (3) In parallel run two paid job ads for a six-week program ($19 an hour in training, $26-27 after) with a $300 budget to measure supply. Pass: at least 5 of 40 sign at $50 or more, at least 3 report a requisition older than 60 days, and at least 40 qualified applicants at under $15 each. Fail: fewer than 2 signed or stated willingness below $44. In between, reprice or retarget (for example dealer groups only) and rerun. Then 90-day gates: three paying pilots at $50+, 80% 90-day retention, at least 24% gross margin on billed hours, workers' comp plus general-liability quote at or below 12% of payroll.

judge_rationales.vc:
This is a decent regional specialty-staffing and training business, not a venture-scale company. I read the first ~9k characters of the dossier (not the full 21k) and scored from the supplied refined idea, both critic rounds and that excerpt.

Size of prize (3): The author puts $100M of revenue at 3-5% unconditional odds, and the second-round critic puts it at 1-2%. At the model's 5-12% EBITDA, $100M of revenue is about $7M of EBITDA on $15-30M of invested capital. Seed investors price on a path to a multi-billion outcome, and this does not offer one. The critic's own number is that realistic EBITDA falls to about zero or negative once free conversion after ~1,000 hours pulls tenure down to 6-12 months. The one real upside is that the hire-train-deploy template could carry over to other shortage trades such as HVAC, electrical, collision and bus. The pitch does not make that case. Comparable staffing and training models (Tradesmen International, Revature, Instawork) either took decades or ended as low-margin businesses.

Why now (5): The shortage is real and chronic, and technician wages are up 14%. PE roll-ups and a tight freight market add some tailwind. The author concedes the 2019 version would also have worked, so there is no sharp inflection. Nothing new (AI, regulation, a new technology) makes this uniquely possible today.

Non-consensus and right (4): The pivot is candid and the diagnosis is sensible, that shops too small to run an academy are stuck. But employer-paid training with a conversion option is an established staffing model. Penske, Love's and Torque already run the in-house version. LAUNCH TransTechs already staffs experienced technicians. The original non-consensus thesis (overnight yard crews at $115 an hour) was killed, and what survives is conventional.

Feasibility and demand (5 and 3): The two-week, under-$500 pre-sale test is cheap, and it is a real strength. Everything that matters is untested:
- No evidence shops buy temporary technicians at scale.
- The $52 bill rate is a 93% markup against a 35-45% staffing norm.
- LAUNCH's implied bill rate for experienced technicians is about $34-39 an hour.
- The customer's premium plus the conversion fee (about $14k) exceeds the $8.2k cost of training a hire directly.
- The WIOA on-the-job-training subsidy is likely barred for hire-out staffing arrangements.
- Trainee-repayment clauses are legally constrained.
- ATRI's shortage statistics measure qualified technicians, not open Level-1 slots.

Defensibility (3): The moat is thin, as the author concedes. Both sides can cut out the bench after a trained worker converts. Torque, Love's and Penske can poach graduates. The likely end state is acquisition by a consolidator.

It would be a fundable small business or an angel or search-fund candidate, not a seed deal top funds would compete for.
judge_rationales.operator:
Scored on the refined Level-1 Bench, not the abandoned yard-crew version. The idea is a decent small business and not venture-scale.

Pain and budget: The pain is real and chronic. ATRI has 19.3% of slots unfilled and 65.5% of shops understaffed, and technician pay is up 14%. The budget line is concrete: an open requisition over 60 days, plus overtime and recruiting spend. The buyer is a small shop owner or service director who signs quickly. That favors a fast first-10-customers motion, and a cohort pilot in one metro costs little.

Demand evidence: This is weaker than the shortage statistics suggest. The 54% and 65.5% figures measure a shortage of qualified technicians. They do not measure demand for temporary six-week-trained Level-1s. The author found no evidence that shops buy temporary technicians at scale. The one temp-tech precedent, LAUNCH TransTechs, sells experienced techs at an apparent bill rate of roughly $34-39. The Bench asks $52 for trainees, which is a 93% markup against a 35-45% norm in skilled-trades staffing.

Substitute: The customer's cheapest alternative is a direct hire at $24-28 plus in-house training, which dealers and fleets already do. The Bench plus the conversion fee costs more than that route. The $7,000 conversion fee "below the $8.2k training cost" argument ignores roughly $14 an hour of premium paid beforehand. Free conversion after about 1,000 hours also pushes rational shops to convert early, which cuts tenure and could take EBITDA to about zero or below.

Unit economics: The author's own base case is 5-12% EBITDA and 7.3% per FTE-year, with breakeven at a $47.50 bill rate. That is thin for a business carrying payroll float, workers' comp on brake and tire work, GL and E&O exposure, and a 30-day free-replacement promise. WIOA OJT subsidies are probably not available for hire-out staffing. Retention clawbacks are legally constrained (DOL v. Smoothstack, California AB 692, New York's Trapped at Work Act). Trainees can be poached by Torque, Love's and Penske. Capital of $15-30M is modest next to the original, but it would produce only about $7M EBITDA at a $100M run-rate.

Upside: Even the author gives about 3-5% odds of $100M, and the critic puts it at 1-2%. The only scale analog, Tradesmen International, took decades. The likely outcome is a $10-25M regional bench-and-train business, sold to a consolidator. It is a real business but not a seed-stage rocket.

Moat and originality: The moat is weak. The model is a known hire-train-deploy staffing pattern, and incumbents (Amerit, Ryder, Penske, Love's) can build academies or price-match. Applying it to heavy-duty trucking shops too small to train their own techs is a sensible niche but not a novel insight.

Why it is not lower: The two-week, under-$500 pre-sale test could resolve the central price question quickly. Staffing demand for technicians demonstrably exists, and a founder can start small with a single academy cohort.
judge_rationales.contrarian:
This is a decent small business, not a venture-scale seed opportunity. Level-1 Bench is the survivor of a pivot that left a thin staffing company, and I scored it as that.

**The insight.** The claim is that the heavy-duty technician shortage is partly a task-allocation and training-capacity problem for shops too small to run an academy. That is a fair observation, but it is not contrarian. Penske's TechStart, Love's apprenticeship, Torque by Ryder and Amerit's academy already act on it, and the source dossier shows they do. The pitch also admits the why-now is moderate. The shortage, 54-65% of shops understaffed, is chronic, so the 2019 version would have worked on the same logic. Wage inflation (14%) and PE roll-ups are real 2025-26 changes, but they cut both ways: they raise the cost of each failed trainee, and they create buyers that will build their own pipelines.

**Economics.** The model depends on a $52 bill rate against a $27 wage, a 93% markup versus a 35-45% norm for skilled-trades staffing. The only temp-technician precedent found, LAUNCH TransTechs, appears to bill about $34-39 for experienced techs. Breakeven is $47.50, so there is little cushion. The second-round critic found two mechanics that appear broken:
- **Conversion fee versus tenure.** The fee falls to zero after about 1,000 hours. A rational shop and worker both convert at 6-12 months, which roughly doubles the graduates needed and pushes EBITDA to about zero or below.
- **WIOA subsidy.** On-the-job-training reimbursement is likely barred for hire-out staffing placements (Iowa policy read this session; other boards per snippets).

The customer's all-in cost at the conversion point (about $14k of premium plus fee) also exceeds the $8.2k they would spend training a green hire directly. Margins are 5-12% EBITDA at best. A staffing business with that margin and a hire-train-deploy retention problem is not what top funds compete for. The DOL's Smoothstack suit and the California and New York limits on training-repayment clauses make lock-in hard.

**Demand.** The shortage statistics measure missing qualified technicians, not demand for temporary six-week-trained Level-1s. Nothing shows shops buy trainee labor at scale. Over 57% of the upside FTEs sit in enterprise accounts that the idea itself says insource. The author puts the odds of $100M at 3-5% unconditional and says the unconditional median is a failed pilot. The critic puts it at 1-2%.

**Defensibility.** The author lists the moat as weak at the start and moderate at best, with no counter-positioning. Consolidators and OEM-linked incumbents can copy it, and the likeliest end state is acquisition by one of them.

**What keeps the score from going lower.** The idea is candid and cheap to test: a roughly $500 pre-sale to 40 targets, plus a measured supply test. Capital is about $15-30M and carries no vans or fleet exposure. It is a plausible $10-25M regional benching and training business with an acquisition exit. It is not a seed-stage bet on a decade-defining company, so I scored it 3, in the "decent small business, not venture-scale" band.

title: Run-Base Shrinker v2: funded retirement of application run cost, paid per invoice line that drops
one_liner: A vendor-neutral company that funds and runs the retirement of unused application run cost (apps, licences, hosting, third-party support, AMS contract lines) and is paid a share only when a third-party invoice line actually falls, on a ledger the client's Internal Audit signs.

critic_top_objection.competition: The incumbents are already conceding the savings the Shrinker would bill for, and the cheapest fix for the 'billed on volume' problem is a contract change, not a 35% third party. Vendors and rivals are moving to fixed-price, outcome-based and productivity-commitment terms. Cognizant says fixed-bid and outcome work is now over 50% of revenue. Rimini Street sells Rimini Manage on a fixed-price, unlimited-ticket model. Rimini also argues in public that time-and-materials AMS has 'no provision for root cause problem management', which is this idea's exact thesis, voiced by a vendor with 3,100 clients. Sourcing advisers are telling buyers to demand front-loaded productivity commitments and a share of the gain at renewal. ISG's Q2 2026 data shows Americas managed-services ACV down 12% to $5.2B, with IT outsourcing down 23% 'led by' application development and maintenance. Industry AI deflation is quoted at 2-5% a year, and a TCS leader reportedly says 10-15% can be committed from day one (unattributed). The gate defines the baseline as 'contract-guaranteed AI pass-through', so the Shrinker only earns beyond what the vendor already concedes. Its 6-12% headroom over 3 years is the same size as the discount the client wins anyway by renegotiating. Under fixed-bid contracts a ticket cut raises the vendor's margin, not the client's saving, until the baseline resets. On the vendor-labor lever the client's real alternative is 'renegotiate or rebid to a fixed-price vendor', which costs 0% of savings.
critic_top_objection.customer: The $100M volume math contradicts the 36-month fee structure, using the gate's own inputs. The offer takes 30-35% of savings for 36 months and then the client keeps 100%. That makes each client a three-year annuity, so concurrent payers equal 3 times new clients per year. The gate says 79 clients is reachable at '12-15 new clients a year'. That produces only 36-45 paying clients, or about $45-57M a year at the gate's $1.26M per client, not $100M. Holding 79 payers needs about 26 new signings every year, sustained. Against the dossier's 300-600 reachable US payers, that is 4-9% of the whole market per year, or roughly 145 cumulative logos (about 25-50% of reachable payers) by year 7. Repeat sales are unlikely to fill the gap because retirements and deletions are one-time savings. On the dossier's evidence-anchored inputs ($0.45M a year per client), $100M needs 222 concurrent payers, about 74 new clients a year. That is 12-25% of the entire market annually, which is not reachable. What survives is a $10-25M project business with a revenue cliff at month 36 on every client. The gate's 'strong' verdict and $110M upside never test this.
critic_top_objection.execution: PRICE AND TIMING: the vendor-labor savings pool is already being harvested, one time and cheaply, by a channel the pitch undervalues. The 30-35% for 36 months has no market support. A sourcing adviser's published Cognizant SAP AMS renewal reports about 16% off contracted fees, a roughly 9% rate-card cut, year-over-year productivity savings layered on top, and more than 40x return on advisory spend (my inference: $19M claimed savings / 40 is about $0.5M of fees, roughly 2.5% of savings). Redress Compliance charges 25% of savings beyond the vendor's best-and-final, invoiced once after signature, no savings no fee, but its page covers software-publisher deals and does not name IT services. HFS says 75% of enterprises want to renegotiate IT services contracts, up from 40% in 2020. By the time the Shrinker has three design partners and a Big-4-style protocol (the gate's own test is 30-60 days, then a 36-month tail), the 2025-27 renewal wave will have taken the first 15-20% of the vendor-labor line, and what is left is the residual 'beyond contract AI pass-through' that the gate's own baseline rule defines. The 'we fund the engineering' justification for the high share is the input losing value fastest: SAP ships a free Custom Code Migration app plus Joule/ABAP AI assistance, and AWS Transform custom and GitHub Copilot app modernization are generally available. The CFO is being asked to pay a third of the savings, for three years, for capital the CFO already has and labor that is getting cheaper.

upside_believable: No. The $100M upside needs several assumptions at once, and the author's own sensitivities show how fragile it is. About 700 reachable payers is unsourced, though the definition is broader than the dossier's 300-600 offshore-labor count, so it is not absurd. Accounts must land at $40M and double to an effective $80M within 3 years. Verified reduction must reach 9% at year 3 and 11.5% at year 5, and the rewrite concedes documented per-client savings of $1-5M a year do not support that. Blended share must be 28%, engineering cost 0.30x, and signings must climb from 3 to 20 a year via channels that are asserted, not owned. Tech E&O and cheap receivables financing must also be available. Any one adverse change drops year-7 revenue below $100M by the rewrite's own numbers: signings down 30% gives $70M, and a $60M effective base gives $76M. These assumptions are correlated, not independent, because they all depend on owner follow-through plus CFO willingness to pay a top-of-range share for a long tail. The 2-4% odds come from the author's own priors and carry no validation. Peak burn of about $32M for the upside versus about $28M for the median looks too low for 94 logos funding roughly $2.8M of engineering each. The gate-and-kill structure is honest and cheap, so the idea is worth testing as an option, but it is not a believable path to a large business as written.
remaining_holes: The core 'why pay us' question is unanswered. The pitch sells 'execution with the CFO behind it', but the CFO is the client, so the missing ingredient is one the buyer already owns. Wave 1 also leads with low-engineering lines (licence, SaaS, hosting, support), where our funding adds nothing. The real comparators are a flat-fee diagnostic from ISG, UpperEdge or Flexera, or Redress at 25% invoiced once. The rewrite's own value claim is 'roughly parity with DIY at observed 25-30% realization'. Parity is not a reason to switch, and the edge depends on realization well above 50%, which is untested.

The price concession is cosmetic. Critique 3 said 30-35% for 3 years (about 0.9-1.05x a year's saving in total fees) was unsupported. v2 charges 30% for 3 years plus 10% for 4 more, which is 1.3x at headline, 1.1x at the 26%/8% median blend and 1.24x at the 28%/10% upside blend. The headline share fell a few points while the buyer's total take stayed the same or rose. The tail was added to fix the volume math, not the buyer's problem, and the 'adds only 12%' framing measures company revenue, not what the buyer pays. The tail is also a fee for keeping a ledger of the client's own invoices.

The dated-event wedge contradicts the fee definition. Verified reduction is the lesser of units x price and the actual net fall in that vendor's invoice. SQL Server 2016 support ended 14 Jul 2026 and Windows Server 2016 ends 12 Jan 2027. I confirmed both dates, and also that these are price-up events: SQL ESU year 1 is about 75% of licence cost, then 150% and 300% (secondary sources, unverified against Microsoft). Retiring a server there avoids new spend, so no invoice line falls. VMware repricing has per-CPU core floors and bundling (consultancy sources), so removing VMs can leave the invoice flat or higher. Under v2's own definition the fee on these triggers is near zero. The post-acquisition trigger has a similar problem: synergy targets are already in the deal model, so baseline fights return.

No new evidence was gathered. Every 'what would change my mind' item from the critics is converted into a plan. The 700-payer count, 9-11.5% verified reduction, CFO acceptance of 26-30% for 3 years plus a tail, tech E&O availability, lender terms at 12% or less and client acceptance of a liability cap all remain unverified. The rewrite's own sizing, 'if under 500, the upside fails', rests on a number it admits it made up.

The 14-day test is weak and does not test the riskiest assumption. It uses a convenience sample of friendly IT-finance and ITAM contacts, and getting three companies to hand over AP exports and SSO logs by cold outreach within 7 days is unlikely. A non-sharing outcome is relabelled 'inconclusive' and a 'demand signal'. The pass metric is business owners emailing back 'agree' to a contact with no budget authority, which is stated intent, not an invoice line falling within 12 months. The real evidence (20% targeted, 5-6% realized) is about follow-through, which a 14-day email poll cannot measure.

The sales cycle and CAC are not resolved. A day-120 gate for a CFO-signed program agreement on a $40M+ base, from a new firm with no references, compares badly with Rimini's 6-12 month cycle for a simpler pitch. The Estate X-ray is 100% credited against success fees, so it is a prepayment, not revenue. The pre-sale delivery cost of $75-150k still exists and is recouped only if the deal signs. 'Pre-sale cost disappears' is overstated.

Moat and liability fixes are asserted, not shown. The outcome-statistics 'cornered resource' relies on contract language giving us ownership of derivatives, while enterprise buyers are inserting no-training and no-derivative clauses. Flexera, ISG and any firm executing retirements would accumulate the same statistics. SOC 1 Type 2 for SOX-scope systems is replaced by 'SOC 2 early', and the 6-12 month observation window is absent from the day-120 and month-12 gates. Client acceptance of a liability cap on production-affecting retirements is assumed.

The pool cross-check is mismatched. It divides by a $40B offshore run-related pool that includes the labor and AMS spend v2 says it will not claim. The headline inputs also do not reconcile with the stated per-client fees: the upside inputs give about $2.6M a year per client against the stated $1.6M peak, so the model has unstated haircuts.

The central case is a thin-margin $17M-revenue services firm that burns about $28M, with a 2-4% unconditional chance of reaching $100M. As a venture that is negative expected value unless the early gates are cheap, so everything rests on the kill gates being enforced. A plain contingent services business is valued low (PRGX comp, about $195M on roughly $165M revenue).
riskiest_assumption: Once a CFO backs the program, business owners will release at least half of the identified retirable run spend, so that third-party invoice lines actually fall within 12 months. Everything downstream (share, funding, tail, financing) needs a fee base that exists. Price has precedent (SaaS-buying share models of 15-30%, recovery audit, cloud savings share); realization has contrary evidence (20% targeted, 5-6% realized in a health-system panel; $1M of labor to save $200k of licences).
two_week_test: 14 days, about $0 cash, no system access, only data the owner is authorised to share under NDA. Days 1-7: recruit one insider advisor (ex-AMS delivery head, ITAM or IT-finance lead); reach out to about 40 people in IT finance, ITAM, vendor management and PE portfolio operations at companies with an estimated $40M+ of external application run spend; offer a free 'retirable spend' list from one export in 48 hours; goal three companies. Days 5-10: from each company's exports (AP lines for software, hosting and support with renewal dates; SSO or usage report; application inventory) build a ranked list of at least 15 units of $25k+ a year with renewal date, usage evidence and named owner; record identified dollars as a share of the base supplied. Days 8-14: the company contact (not us) emails each unit's owner 'we plan to retire or downsize this on [renewal date] unless you object by [date]'; count responses by dollars (written agree, silent, object). In the same window show the CFO or Controller the one-page term sheet (share, tail, buyout, sweep) and record the maximum share they would sign, the paying budget line, the alternative they would use (Redress, in-house, vendor) and which event would make them sign within 90 days. PASS (all three): M1 identified dollars at least 6% of the supplied base in at least 2 of 3 companies; M2 written agreement on at least 50% of identified dollars and objection on no more than 25%; M3 at least 2 of 3 finance contacts state a maximum share of 25% or more on invoice-evidenced lines and name the paying budget. KILL: identified under 4% in two of three, or agreement under 25% of dollars, or finance caps at 15% or prefers in-house or Redress. INCONCLUSIVE: fewer than three companies agree to share data in 7 days (itself a demand signal); then run the fallback of 12 calls with people who ran decommissioning programs (dollars identified, retired and actually dropped from invoices; median realization under 30% means kill) plus two independent counts of qualifying US companies from former AMS delivery heads. Later gates, kill not shrink: day 60 two paid X-rays at $50k+; day 120 one signed program agreement at 25%+ share on a $40M+ base signed by a CFO or Controller; month 6 tech E&O quote of $5M+ with no AI exclusion on human-led work; month 12 first audited invoice drops with at least 50% of Wave 1 dollars realized; miss any two by month 12 and stop.

judge_rationales.vc:
Prize: this is a contingent-fee services company, not software. The author's own median is about $17M revenue in year 7 with thin margins and about $28M of burn. The $100M case needs about five correlated assumptions at once: 700 reachable payers (unsourced), accounts doubling to $80M, 9-11.5% verified reduction, 28% share and 20 signings a year. The author puts it at 2-4% unconditional. The closest scaled comp, PRGX, sold for about $195M, and Ameresco runs about 12% EBITDA on a heavy balance sheet. A seed fund needs a credible path to a $1B+ outcome, and this offers a tiny tail. It is a decent small business with an unusually honest kill-gate plan, and that honesty lowers the venture score because it confirms the ceiling.

Why-now: the reasons are moderate and mixed. AI lowers retirement engineering cost, but the same tools are cheap for clients, who can do the work in-house (Citi). CFO pressure for AI offsets and the lack of a neutral referee for AI savings (ISG) are real. The dated-event wedge undercuts itself. SQL Server and Windows Server end-of-support and VMware repricing are price-up events, so under v2's own fee definition (the lesser of units removed times price and the actual net fall in the invoice) the invoice line often does not fall. The SAP wedge was already dropped. The post-acquisition trigger runs into synergy numbers already in the deal model, which brings back baseline fights.

Originality: the slot of vendor-neutral, funded, paid only on an invoice-line drop is genuinely open, and no ESCO-for-IT exists. But the dossier warns it may be open because the economics are hard. The critics also showed that the pitch is crowded: Redress, Flexera, ISG, Rimini, AMS self-funding and AI-SRE vendors all sit nearby. The unit-of-account fix (units times price, not baseline) is a clever design, not a non-consensus insight about the world.

Feasibility: this is the weakest point. The customer must have a CFO sign, owners release spend, Internal Audit accept the ledger and the client's change process execute, and the firm must carry production-change liability with unproven E&O cover and no SOC 1 path. The evidence for realization is bad (20% targeted, 5-6% realized). The sales cycle is likely 9-18 months for a new firm with no references, and the Estate X-ray is credited, so it is a prepayment and not margin. The 14-day test cannot measure follow-through, which is the riskiest assumption. Capital need is heavy ($28-60M) against equity-like receivables.

Defensibility: no power is strong at launch. Counter-positioning holds only against AMS vendors. The outcome-statistics moat conflicts with no-training and no-derivative clauses. Flexera, ISG and any executing firm can collect the same statistics. The ledger as standard is speculative. The tail adds only about 12% to revenue and is a fee for keeping a record of the client's own invoices.

Demand: there is no RFP, precedent or CFO letter showing anyone will pay 26-30% for 3 years plus a 10% tail. That is about 1.1-1.3x annual savings, versus Redress at 25% once or a flat-fee diagnostic. The v2 value claim is roughly parity with doing it yourself. The only quantified evidence on follow-through is negative. Zero validation has been gathered; every critic request was converted into a plan.

Net: a thoughtful, well-gated small services bet that a seed fund would pass on. A pass is the correct call unless an early gate (owner release above 50% of identified dollars plus CFO sign at 25%+ share) is cleared first.
judge_rationales.operator:
Scored as a serial founder of profitable companies. This is a decent small business at best, not venture-scale.

PAIN: Cost-out is a real CFO theme. Event-driven entry (post-merger synergy windows, pre-exit EBITDA, end-of-support) is the best part of the refined idea. But retiring applications is chronic and important, not urgent. The dossier's one realization data point is a 20% target that delivered 5-6%, and business owners resist. The refined idea names owner release of funds as its riskiest assumption and has not tested it.

FIRST 10 CUSTOMERS IN 6-12 MONTHS: The paid Estate X-ray ($75-150k, 100% credited) can plausibly win a few buyers, and PE operating partners and integration offices are reachable. But a CFO-signed program agreement with a 30% share for 3 years plus a tail, from a firm with no references, will probably take 9-18 months. First success-fee dollars arrive around month 9-15 at best. The critic is right that the credited X-ray is prepayment, not margin, and that pre-sale delivery cost still exists.

UNIT ECONOMICS: These are weak and fragile. The buyer pays about 1.1-1.3x a year's savings for work that is roughly parity with doing it yourself, so the 'why pay us' question is unanswered. The wedge also contradicts the fee definition. SQL Server and Windows Server end-of-support and VMware repricing are price-up events, so retiring units there avoids new spend rather than dropping an invoice line. Under the idea's own definition, the fee on those triggers is near zero. Engineering is funded up front against disputable, contingent receivables, valued like PRGX (about $195M on about $165M of revenue). The model's own median is $17M of revenue in year 7 with about $28M of burn, which is poor capital efficiency. The upside needs about 700 payers (unsourced), accounts that double, 9-11.5% reduction (documented savings are $1-5M per client, which does not support that), and 20 signings a year. Any one miss drops year-7 revenue below $100M, and the author puts the odds at 2-4%.

WHAT IS GOOD: Real, honest gating. A cheap 14-day test, plus kill gates at day 60, day 120 and month 12. A defensible unit of account (a third-party invoice line that falls). The slot between Redress, Flexera, ISG and the AMS vendors is genuinely unoccupied. The ledger could become a standard. The X-ray is a legitimate consulting wedge that could fund a small profitable firm.

WHAT IS BAD: Moat is weak. Counter-positioning holds only against AMS vendors on scope removal. The outcome-statistics moat conflicts with buyers' no-training and no-derivative clauses. Incumbents and AI tooling make execution cheap for clients. SOC 1 timing, liability caps and tech E&O are unproven, and no new evidence was gathered; every open item became a plan. Demand evidence is thin: no RFPs, no LOIs, no precedent for a vendor-neutral party paid a share of application run savings for 3 years or more.

Seed-stage calibration: a 4 means decent but not a deal top funds would compete for. As a serial founder I would run the 14-day test because it costs about nothing. I would not commit capital to the funded-retirement model before seeing signed CFO paper.
judge_rationales.contrarian:
The insight is real. Savings that get identified but never executed, because nobody is paid to switch things off, is a true gap. The 5-6% realized against 20% targeted evidence supports it. Pricing on third-party invoice lines that actually fall is a cleaner unit of account than the usual baseline fight. The dossier also found no one selling vendor-neutral, engineering-funded, invoice-verified retirement. But the idea is weak as a seed-stage venture bet, for four reasons.

1. The economics are unconvincing. A CFO who has already backed the program pays about 1.1-1.3x a year's savings in fees, and the author's own value claim is "roughly parity with DIY". The tail was added to fix the company's volume math, not the buyer's problem. Wave 1 leads with low-engineering lines (licence, SaaS, hosting, support), where funding adds nothing. Those lines are also where Redress (25% of savings), Flexera, ISG and in-house teams already sit.

2. The dated-event wedge contradicts the fee definition. SQL Server and Windows Server end-of-support and VMware repricing are price-up events. Retiring a server there avoids new spend, so no invoice line falls and the fee is near zero. Post-merger synergies are already in the deal model, so baseline fights return.

3. The numbers describe a thin-margin services firm. The median is about $17M revenue with about $28M burned. The author puts odds of $100M at 2-4%, and it fails if any single assumption moves. Contingent services revenue is valued low (PRGX sold for about $195M). Capital needs are venture-sized but the margins are services-grade. That is a decent small business, not a Stripe, Toast or Samsara.

4. Demand is unproven and the moat is thin. There is no RFP, no LOI and no precedent of a vendor-neutral third party collecting a share of audited run savings. The 700-payer count is invented, and the 14-day test measures stated intent from a friendly sample, not savings that actually reach invoices. The moat is asserted at best. Outcome statistics run into no-training clauses, and competitors could accumulate the same data. Tech E&O cover for production changes by AI agents is untested.

What keeps this from a 1-2 is that the gates are cheap and honest, and the central observation about the execution gap is true. Whether it becomes a funded-execution business or a smaller, contested licence-savings business is unknown.

title: Root-Cause Contract: outcome-priced fixes for social housing's costliest homes
one_liner: We find the 5-8% of a social landlord's homes that keep failing for the same physical reason, fix the cause, and are paid against what an untreated control group actually costs, climbing from a 50-home sprint to multi-year capitated contracts financed by third-party capital.

critic_top_objection.competition: The strongest incumbent already sells the adjacent product and already holds everything the entrant would need to borrow. Wates launched 'Healthy Homes' in April 2024, a dedicated damp-and-mould and disrepair-reduction service, delivered with its own labour, with six customers already signed. Wates says it manages repairs for 500,000+ homes across 65 social landlords. The gate and the dossier both missed this. Mears has said regulation is creating new damp, mould and condensation service lines [S], and it is winning 10-year total-asset deals: Rooftop is GBP15M a year for 7,000 units (about GBP2,143 a home) and Birmingham is GBP45M a year for 11,500 units (about GBP3,913 a home), both covering far more than repairs. The hot-spot fee the idea wants (about GBP2,200 per costly home) is about what Mears is already paid per average home for everything. A landlord on price-per-property can tell its prime to fix the root causes at no extra fee. A landlord on visit-priced contracts can write a hot-spot lot or pain/gain schedule into its next tender or an amendment. The likely incumbent response is cheap: add a gain-share schedule, bundle sensors and analytics, and price it as part of the existing contract. The incumbent wins because it already has the job-level data, the vans, the tenant access and the landlord relationship. The entrant would depend on a landlord handing over data and a cohort carved out of the incumbent's contract, and on the incumbent not objecting. Scattered single homes across a patch give the entrant no route density, so the likely end state is subcontracting to the prime at prime-level margins (Mears guides to 5.0-5.2% for FY26, 5-6% medium term) rather than 12-18%.
critic_top_objection.customer: NO EVIDENCE ANYONE WILL BUY THIS, AND BUYER BEHAVIOUR POINTS THE OTHER WAY. Landlords are bundling everything into whole-stock deals and insourcing for control, not carving out their worst homes for a risk-taker. Bundling: Livin (about GBP200M, 10 years, single lot, TAC-1 alliance covering responsive, voids, adaptations, compliance, planned, retrofit, cyclical; award notice 27 Feb 2026), Thurrock (GBP240M), Winchester (GBP56.7M, scope names disrepair and damp-and-mould work types), PfH GBP480M and Riverside GBP657M frameworks. Insourcing: Teign Housing is ending a 10-year Ian Williams contract in April 2027 so it has 'more control over how we work' [V]; Grand Union, Uttlesford, Basildon, Ashford, Cheshire West. The signer (FD/Director of Assets, then board) would be paid roughly a 20% saving on the cohort (about GBP560 a home, about GBP1.1M on 2,000 homes, under 0.5% of a 40,000-home landlord's turnover [A]) while the landlord stays the s10A duty holder with the full legal, Ombudsman and reputational tail on its most vulnerable, most litigated homes. The Ombudsman's Hyde investigation blamed failure to oversee contractors. That is a bad risk/reward for a career-risk-averse buyer. The fee also draws on three budget owners (responsive, disrepair/legal, capital) [A], so there is no single owner with a budget line and a burning need. Demand shown in the dossier is for works and software (Mobysoft GBP97-276k a year, Wigan GBP2M, InCommunities GBP3M), never for capitation. Absence of any carve-out precedent after about 10 targeted searches is consistent with buyers not wanting it, not only with a gap.
critic_top_objection.execution: A newco cannot get through the procurement door, and the scope is already taken. Landlords are bundling disrepair and damp-and-mould work into single long-term repairs partners, so a carve-out of the worst homes sits inside someone else's exclusive scope. Winchester (tender published 15 Oct 2025, go-live 1 Aug 2026, GBP56.7M, 4+3 years) puts day-to-day repairs, disrepair and damp-and-mould work in one contract. It requires turnover of at least 1.5x annual contract value, EL GBP10M / PL GBP10M / PI GBP5M, and a Dun & Bradstreet failure score of 51 or more because it is rated a high-risk procurement. Livin Housing, with only about 8,500 homes, is tendering one fully integrated repairs, maintenance and compliance partner: GBP200M, 10 years from April 2026, turnover of at least GBP40M against GBP20M a year. A 500-home pilot at about GBP1.1M a year needs about GBP1.65M of trading history and a D&B score that a company with no accounts cannot produce. So the realistic entry is as a subcontractor to the prime, who is then both the channel and the competitor. The notice-to-go-live gap at Winchester was about 9.5 months, so a contract signed from a start now goes live in late 2027. The 2026-2031 round is already awarded: Mears-Thurrock 5+5 years, Cardo-Dacorum 10 years, the PfH GBP480M framework, Riverside to about 2029.

upside_believable: No. The upside needs six conditions to hold together: a 25%-plus cost share at the top 5-8% with 60%-plus persistence, a causal cut of 45%-plus after a winter, a new outcome-priced hot-spot lot appearing in 2029-33 tenders, GBP20-30M of fund capital raised on a thin evidence base, four primes choosing to subcontract rather than build in-house, and 60-70% renewal with no insourcing. Even generous independent odds (0.5 on the cut, 0.25 on category creation, 0.6 on capital, 0.5 on primes, 0.7 on renewal) put the conditional probability near 2-3%, not 10-15%, and overall under 1% against the stated 3-5%. The revenue arithmetic itself checks out (GBP49.7M + 15.2M + 16.5M + 1M = GBP82.4M, about $107M at 1.3), but it requires about 27% of reachable counterparties by year 7, which the rewrite itself calls heroic. It prices cohort homes at a per-home fee that assumes near-total persistence while the gate allows 60%, and it counts about 20% of revenue as GBP5,500-a-home pass-through works with blended EBITDA of only 8-12%. The credible residual is a small specialist niche: rungs one to three plus a few prime or insourcing fix-only deals, plausibly low single-digit GBP millions, in line with the dossier's $13M median and $58M upside rather than $100M.
remaining_holes: Pricing contradicts the pitch. The headline says we are paid against an untreated control group, but the rung-four fee is 85% of the cohort's own 36-month trailing cost, rebased and multiplied by the landlord's rest-of-stock cost index. That is the trailing-baseline pricing the rewrite says it dropped, with an inflation index added. Once a landlord hands over its whole cohort there is no untreated same-profile group left, so a concurrent control cannot exist at the capitated rung.

The claim that the indexed fee does not pay us for what analytics vendors deliver only holds inside the randomised trial. Mobysoft-style repeat-visit cuts land mostly in the hot homes, not in a rest-of-stock average, so the index does not strip them out. Critic 1's cheap-25% point is answered at rung three and not at rung four.

Per-home fee and persistence are inconsistent. Upside revenue uses about GBP2,300 per home, which assumes the cohort stays near GBP2,700-2,800 a year. The pass gate only requires 60% persistence, which implies a counterfactual near GBP1,700. A control-based fee at 85% of that is about GBP1,430 a home, roughly 38% less recurring revenue. The GBP2,800 cohort cost is also self-described as unsourced.

Randomised waitlist controls collide with Awaab's Law. Phase 2 commentary (Clyde & Co and others; I did not read the gov.uk text) says supplementary works to prevent recurrence must start within 5 working days of the investigation, with 12 weeks as the backstop. Withholding root-cause works from control homes for a winter is legally exposed wherever a qualifying hazard is reported, and invites disrepair claims. The rewrite does not address this.

Rung three has no procurement route. 400 homes at about GBP3,000 each is about GBP1.2M, well above the roughly GBP207k-213k services threshold the rewrite relies on for the 50-home sprint. The capitated rung is a full flexible-procedure tender with turnover tests of about 1.5-2x annual contract value, which Critic 3 raised; the rewrite answers only with 'parent-guarantee provider'. Below-threshold relief is real (s.85 Procurement Act bars suitability or turnover gates on regulated below-threshold contracts) and helps rung two, but does not extend to rungs three or four.

The prime channel is declared, not shown. No prime has been asked, and primes such as Wates already sell root-cause fixes with direct labour. At GBP1,900 a home, break-even is roughly a 40% cut with a landlord-funded fix and roughly 55% with a newco-funded one, and the prime keeps the spread. No unit economics are given for the GBP15.2M of upside revenue from this channel.

Capitated economics worsen over time. The fee glides from 85% to 75%, which pushes the provider-funded break-even cut from about 40% to about 48%. The upside assumes a 45% cut, so at year 5 it still loses money if the provider funds the fix. The rewrite's quoted 43% break-even also does not reconcile to its own inputs (I get about 39.5% at 85%).

Buyer pull for the capitated rung has no new evidence. The rewrite removes the uncapped guarantee and puts claims outside the fee, so the landlord keeps the full s10A tail and the saving shrinks from 20% to 15%, which makes the finance-director risk/reward worse. The answer is only that the landlord will buy after seeing its own trial. I found no outcome-priced or gain-share damp-and-mould contract; landlords buy remediation by direct award from Fusion21 or PfH frameworks, where the newco is not listed.

Rungs two and three compete head-on with Wates Healthy Homes (direct labour, root-cause fixes, no 2026 data found) and framework suppliers. A 24-month re-performance warranty is table stakes against Airtech's three-year and EnviroVent's ten-year guarantees, and a free ledger x-ray is what Mobysoft already sells.

Internal sizing inconsistency. The rewrite says a price-per-property book yields a cohort of 500-600 homes, yet the upside has four prime-channel books of 2,000 homes each, which needs each prime to aggregate three or four landlord contracts, each consenting to the variation. The counterparty count of 19 also does not match the stated components (12 + 4 = 16, plus unspecified fix-only customers).
The $17M median is conditional on passing the data gate (30%) and the first trial. The unconditional median outcome is the kill, at zero revenue, so the label flatters the case.
The gate's failure condition conflates two questions: fewer than 2 ledgers by day 28 would kill the idea on a data-sharing failure, which is different from whether the hot-spot cohort exists.
riskiest_assumption: That the same 5-8% of homes, selected on repeat same-fault jobs, carry at least 25% of repair-plus-disrepair spend and still cost at least 60% of their prior level the following year (persistent and therefore fixable, not regression-to-the-mean noise), and that a real landlord will hand over the ledger to find out. Everything downstream (margin, landlord value, the case for a fund, a priced tail) depends on it, nobody has measured it, and it is cheap to test. The next-riskiest assumption, a 40%+ causal cut against a concurrent control, cannot be tested without a winter.
two_week_test: Build the x-ray (top-5% share, year-to-year persistence, same-fault share, cluster index, data-quality score) in days 1-2. On day 1 file an FOI to 25 councils for anonymised per-property totals for the 100 costliest homes in 2023/24 to 2025/26 (answers arrive after the window, for the 8-week gate). Days 2-4 contact 40 named targets: 15 Directors or Heads of Asset or Repairs at 25k+ associations and ALMOs, 10 council housing directors, 8 contract directors at second-tier PfH-lot primes, 7 at insourcing landlords. Offer a free 48-hour x-ray under NDA with hashed property IDs. Ask three questions: does your repairs contract allow a cohort variation, which budget line pays for supplementary root-cause works, and would you fund a 50-home sprint from it if the x-ray justifies it. Day-14 readout: at least 8 of 40 reply, at least 2 ledgers promised in writing, at least 1 received and analysed, at least 1 verbal willingness to fund a sprint. Eight-week pass: at least 3 ledgers covering 40k+ homes, top-5% share of 25% or more in at least 2, persistence of 60% or more. Kill: top-5% share under 15% in two of three, persistence under 40%, or fewer than 2 ledgers by day 28 (nobody will even share data, which answers the demand question). Cost: analyst time and about GBP15-25k of counsel.

judge_rationales.vc:
Score: 3 overall, a decent specialist niche business rather than a venture-scale company.

SIZE OF PRIZE (3). The addressable pool is about GBP570-620M a year of spend landlords already make, in one country and one sub-segment. The pitch's own odds are 3-5% of reaching $100M a year. The second-round critic's independent estimate is under 1%, because six conditions have to hold together: the cost concentration, a 45%+ causal cut, new tenders that price against a control, GBP20-30M of fund capital, primes subcontracting rather than building in-house, and renewals. Even the $107M upside case relies on about 27% of reachable counterparties, which the pitch itself calls heroic. About 20% of that revenue is GBP5,500-a-home pass-through works. Blended EBITDA is 8-12% (Mears earns about 5.7%). The equity story therefore rests on a "fund and protocol layer" that does not exist yet. The credible outcome is a low-single-digit GBP million specialist firm, in line with the dossier's $13M median and $58M upside. No seed fund underwrites that as a venture return. Stripe, Toast and Samsara had a plausible path to a very large outcome at founding, and this does not.

WHY NOW (6). Awaab's Law phase 2 starts 30 Nov 2026. Guidance requires works that prevent recurrence. Claimant costs are uncapped to at least Oct 2028. Sector cash interest cover is 59%, repairs spend is forecast up 14%, and only 4% of landlords call themselves very prepared. All of that is real and primary-sourced. But the same shock raises the cost base, pushes insourcing (Teign, Basildon, Cheshire West, Hyde), and turns root-cause works into a statutory per-case step inside every incumbent's contract. The Decent Homes Standard 2035 criterion is no forcing function. The rung-four capitated market is a 2029-31 event the company would have to help create. So the timing is good for rungs one to three and speculative for the rung that carries about 79% of the upside revenue.

NON-CONSENSUS AND RIGHT (6). Control-indexed pricing, the stepped-wedge randomised trial and the regression-to-the-mean discipline (Camden hotspotting is the right analog) are genuinely sharp. The honest odds and the kill gate are unusually disciplined. But being right is unproven. Mobysoft and Switchee sell the easy 25% cheaply. Wates Healthy Homes already sells root-cause fixes for damp and mould. Price-per-property primes already take capitated risk. Landlords asked to carve out their worst homes are bundling, insourcing, or selling and regenerating the negative-value ones. The final pricing still contradicts the pitch: the rung-four fee is built on trailing cost with an index, and a concurrent control cannot exist once a landlord hands over its whole cohort. The pitch is paid against a control only at rung three.

DEFENSIBILITY (3). The pitch says there is no moat on day one. The reachable moats are a causal-effects library after about three winters and a verification standard adopted by a third party, and both are speculative. The protocol is easy to copy once published, and Wates or Mears could add a gain-share schedule. The 24-month warranty is table stakes against Airtech's three-year and EnviroVent's ten-year guarantees.

FEASIBILITY (4). The 8-week test costs under GBP25k and the staged ladder is smart. But the 50-home sprint is the only rung with a clean procurement route (below the GBP207,720 services threshold, with s.85 relief). The 400-home trial (about GBP1.2M) and the capitated tender face full flexible-procedure turnover and D&B tests that a newco cannot meet. Randomised waitlist controls collide with Awaab's Law, because withholding preventive works from control homes is legally exposed. The prime channel is unasked. Capitation needs a stop-loss that does not exist, and the landlord keeps the s10A tail. Sales cycles run 14+ months. Break-even needs a 40-48% cut when the provider funds the fix, against a measured 25% from analytics alone.

EVIDENCE OF DEMAND (3). Landlords demonstrably pay for damp-and-mould works and analytics (Wigan about GBP2M, InCommunities about GBP3M, Mobysoft GBP97-276k a year). No landlord is known to buy a cohort carve-out, outcome-priced or capitated, and every observed buyer behaviour points to bundling or insourcing. The load-bearing fact, that the top 5-8% of homes carry 25%+ of spend persistently, is unmeasured. Public Thurrock data suggests broad concentration (27% of homes with 5+ repairs) rather than a sharp tail. The per-home fee also depends on persistence. The gate allows 60%, which implies a counterfactual near GBP1,700 and about 38% less recurring revenue than the upside assumes. The idea does deserve credit for its cheap, falsifiable first test.

NET: fundable as a small bootstrapped or angel-backed venture, or as a services-plus-data spin-out. Not a deal a top seed fund competes for.
judge_rationales.operator:
Score reflects the opportunity as a founder of profitable companies would see it, after reading the dossier, the refined pitch and both critique rounds.

What is real. There is urgent, budgeted pain. Awaab's Law phase 2 starts 30 Nov 2026, claimant costs are uncapped to at least Oct 2028, and landlords already spend visibly on damp and mould (Wigan about GBP2M, InCommunities about GBP3M). Demand-side skew in repairs is plausible. The ladder is sensible: a free ledger x-ray, then a roughly GBP150k sprint under the procurement threshold, then a controlled trial. That is the right way to dodge the fatal "nobody buys capitation" objection, and the 8-week, under-GBP25k kill gate is capital-efficient. The refined version also conceded the right things (trailing-baseline pricing, uncapped guarantee, cornered-data moat).

Why it stays at 4. First, the first customers are plausible but not likely at the 10 mark. Two to four sprint customers in 12 months is believable. Ten is not, because UK housing sales cycles run 6 to 18 months, data-sharing and GDPR friction is real, and PfH itself says pilots rarely convert. Second, the pitch is internally inconsistent where it matters most. Rung four prices at 85% of the cohort's own rebased trailing cost times a rest-of-stock index. That is trailing-baseline pricing, and no concurrent untreated control can exist once the landlord hands over the whole cohort. Randomised waitlist controls also collide with Awaab's Law duties to do supplementary works to prevent recurrence. Third, rungs three and four have no clean procurement route: 400 homes at about GBP3k is about GBP1.2M, well over the roughly GBP207k threshold, and a capitated tender brings turnover tests of about 1.5 to 2x contract value. Fourth, unit economics are thin and worsen over time. Break-even cuts are about 40 to 48% when the provider funds the fix, against a measured analytics-only 25%. The upside revenue assumes about GBP2,300 a home, while the 60% persistence gate implies a fee nearer GBP1,430. About 79% of upside revenue sits in the capitated rung that Critic 2 called unbuyable. Blended EBITDA is only 8 to 12%.

Venture-scale view. The idea states its own odds at 3 to 5% for $100M, and the critic's compounding puts that under 1%. The honest outcome is a niche remediation and verification business at low single-digit GBP millions. The dossier's $13M median and $58M upside describe a decent specialist services firm, not a seed-stage outlier. Moat is none on day one. The aspirational library of measured effects and the verification protocol are years away and could be absorbed by Wates, Mears or Mobysoft, who hold the data and the vans. Rung four also needs GBP20-40M of balance-sheet capital. Managed-care capitation analogs such as Cano Health are cautionary, not encouraging.

Timing is the best dimension: the Awaab's Law catalyst is real and dated, though incumbents and frameworks are absorbing it. Originality is above average thanks to control-indexed outcome pricing and the fix, dispose or regenerate triage. A cheap, fast kill gate and a credible small-business floor stop this from scoring lower. By the calibration scale it is a 3 to 4 (decent small business, not venture-scale), and I land at 4 because the early rungs are budget-funded and cheap to test.
judge_rationales.contrarian:
The insight is real and somewhat non-obvious. Repair demand is skewed. Responsive contractors are paid per visit, so nobody is paid to fix root causes. Awaab's Law phase 2 (30 Nov 2026) makes recurrence legally expensive, with claimant costs uncapped to at least Oct 2028. The strongest part of the refined idea is paying against a randomised concurrent control rather than a trailing baseline. That is a genuine methodological edge, the Camden hotspotting analogy is the right one, and a verified-effects library could become a bankable standard in the way IPMVP did for energy savings. The 8-week, under-GBP25k kill test is also admirable.

As a seed deal it is a small business, not venture scale. The pass probability on the first gate is about 30%, and the stated 3-5% odds of reaching $100M are probably still generous. The second-round critic's chain of independent conditions (45%+ causal cut, a new outcome-priced lot appearing in tenders, GBP20-30M of fund capital, primes choosing to subcontract, 60-70% renewal) puts the overall odds nearer 1%. The dossier's own range, about $13M median and $58M upside, is the more credible ceiling. Blended EBITDA of 8-12% is services-grade, since about 20% of upside revenue and much of the rest is pass-through works. The equity story depends on a fund and protocol layer that does not exist yet. The market is UK-only, with roughly 45-55 reachable large landlords, and the buyer pool is bundling into price-per-property contracts and insourcing (Teign, Hyde, Basildon). Few investors would back that at seed.

The rewrite honestly concedes most of the original fatal flaws: the trailing-cost pricing, the uncapped guarantee, and the moat claims. The second critic's remaining holes are serious, though:
- Once a landlord hands over its whole cohort there is no untreated control left, so the capitated fee falls back to a trailing-baseline price.
- Randomised waitlist controls collide with Awaab supplementary-works clocks.
- The 400-home trial is about GBP1.2M, well above the procurement threshold the sprint relies on.
- The capitated fee persistence and break-even maths do not reconcile.
- The prime channel is declared, not shown.

Demand evidence is thin. Landlords pay for works and software (Wigan GBP2M, InCommunities GBP3M), but nobody has been found paying for cohort risk transfer or outcome-priced damp-and-mould contracts. Wates Healthy Homes already sells root-cause fixes with its own labour. Mobysoft already sells the ledger analysis cheaply.

What survives is a specialist remediation and verification niche, plausibly low single-digit GBP millions. It is worth a cheap test but not a decade-defining seed deal.

title: Qualified-challenger fiscal agent: buy the ticket in choice markets, bid the statewide auctions later
one_liner: Buy two or three owner-operated Medicaid fiscal agents in enrollment and rate-card markets to acquire the scarce asset (multi-state qualification), run them on rented software with a measured exception-rate program, then bid mid-size statewide RFPs and plan-delegated contracts.

critic_top_objection.competition: The entry ticket is held by funded incumbents, and capital is flooding in. New York's RFP required a statewide FI contract elsewhere and a $100M line of credit (dossier, Holland & Knight). Every award the dossier found went to a multi-state incumbent. The 'buy a small FI for past performance' route then competes with H.I.G. (GT Independence, 50k+ participants, Nov 2025) and General Atlantic, which closed a roughly $3B purchase of TEAM Services from Alpine in April 2026 at about 10x EBITDA. TEAM sells financial management services for consumer-directed care. I could not confirm that Acumen sits inside TEAM; the dossier's link rests on an unopened CB Insights page. Acumen itself reports 22-23 states and 100+ programs. A first-time consolidator buys against 10x-multiple sponsors. The only cheap targets are the money-losing ones, since the four Wisconsin FEAs lost 12.5% in aggregate. A new entrant would end up buying either an overpriced or a sick asset.
critic_top_objection.customer: The 'payroll-certainty SLA' is not the vendor's to deliver, and no buyer pays a premium for it. Connecticut is the live test: GT Independence (the 'best operator' in this dossier) still had hundreds of aides with missing, delayed or partial pay in Nov 2025 to Feb 2026. GT says it 'can only execute payments when the state green-lights the funds'. The state (DSS) blames its own incomplete or miscalculated authorization files, plus employers exceeding monthly hours (10% of self-directing employers). The union won a partial settlement of just under $1M in backpay, and the state, not the vendor, was left holding the political problem. If the FI guarantees payroll anyway, it becomes an unsecured lender against hours the state later refuses to reimburse. Arithmetic (A): if just 1% of payroll fronted is unreimbursable, that is about $30 per participant-month at New York's ~$36k per participant-year, or 37% of an $80 fee. In Wisconsin (~$51.7k per participant-year) it is about $43, or 56% of the $76.50 fee. The buyer side also already treats payroll timeliness as a penalty clause, not a priced feature (Wisconsin's contract allows withholding fees for missed payroll; Connecticut has 'enhanced contract monitoring' and a 2026 late-pay penalty bill). In Kentucky, the one live RFP, the state's own FAQ says financial management agencies may bill claims before paying PDS employees, so there is no payroll float for a backstop to cover. Pitch failure mode: the SLA is either un-backable (state-caused misses) or un-monetizable (table stakes).
critic_top_objection.execution: TIMING: the why-now is mostly spent and the one open door is not enterable. As of 2026-10-18: New York is locked to PPL (sole FI since 2025-04-01, award upheld on appeal Oct 2025, no rebid found). West Virginia was awarded in 2024. Wisconsin gave PPL a notice of intent on 2026-01-29 with a protest review still unresolved on a DHS page last revised 2026-10-08, and transfers not before 2027. Ohio DODD closed 2026-01-14 and Alabama FMS RFP 2026-03 closed in June 2025 with multi-award and no award found. That leaves Kentucky (due 2026-11-06, 19 days from now): the listing is a re-procurement of a 2018 RFP, carries stale 2018 text, names no incumbent, participant count or value, and Kentucky is mid-transition of PDS oversight to waiver operating agencies by 2027-01-01. A not-yet-formed company cannot assemble past performance, an EVV integration, a bid lead and a funded payroll line in 19 days. The realistic cycle is RFP to first revenue of about 2 years (Wisconsin: RFP S-1640, NOI Jan 2026, protest open 8+ months, go-live 2027), all pre-revenue burn. Entry requires past performance, which means buying an FI, which means bidding against H.I.G. (GT Independence, Nov 2025), DW Healthcare/Linden (PPL, $425M refinanced in 2025) and General Atlantic (bought TEAM Services, a home-care and payroll platform that includes FMS, for about $3B including debt at about 10x EBITDA, April 2026).

upside_believable:
No. The $103M case needs at least five things to hold together and several are weakly evidenced or contradicted.
(1) $150 blended PMPM on 28k choice participants. The rate-card evidence is $103 (CO), $114-121 (TX; proposed $120.55 in 2024), and $106 (LA). The only prices near $150 are Minnesota's, where the fee is participant-paid out of the care budget and tiers down to $50-155 at the smaller nonprofit providers. A realistic $110-120 on that segment gives about $37-40M, not $50M, and the total falls to about $90M with NY and about $80M without it.
(2) 79k participants in 7 years. That is 1.6x the footprint GT built over about 21 years with H.I.G. capital, delivered here by a handful of acquisitions of 2-6k-participant operators plus unspecified organic growth in markets where PPL, Palco, GT and Acumen already operate.
(3) Winning two mid-size statewide RFPs as a first-time winner while the plan itself says about one competitive award occurs per year nationally.
(4) A New York slot opening through unconfirmed litigation or legislation.
(5) $60-75M of capital available for a business whose median case yields about 5-8% on invested capital.
The probabilities of 8-10% for the upside, about 45% for the median and 40-45% for the bear are reasonably candid, but the upside is a joint event of several low-probability conditions, so 8-10% is probably generous. And even if the upside is hit, the return is roughly 1.4-2.1x over about 7 years. The upside is not believable and, if achieved, not attractive on a capital basis. The idea is worth only the two-week test and a harder look at Minnesota, Texas and Colorado specifics before anything else.
remaining_holes: The premium-price evidence is cherry-picked and partly mis-specified. In Minnesota's CFSS budget model the FMS fee is negotiated with each participant and paid out of the participant's own service budget, not by the state or a plan (MN DHS provider pages, search summary). It is tiered by budget size, not flat. Listed fees run $50-150 at MRCI, $110-150 at Lifeworks, $135-155 at PICS, $50 then $165 at GT, $165 at Accra and $200-400 at Aspen. The '$165-250' figure is the top of the range, and the small nonprofit operators the plan wants to buy charge less. A $150 blended fee on 28k participants has no support, and the 'payer and signer' section is wrong for the single biggest line in the upside.

Colorado is mislabeled as an enrollment market. HCPF ran a 2023-24 RFP and awarded FMS contracts for five years starting 2024-07-01 (HCPF IM 24-003, search summary; PDF returned 403, so awardee names are unconfirmed). Participants choose only among the awarded vendors, which in 2025 were Palco and PPL at $103.21 each. A new entrant can reach Colorado only by buying a contract holder, which is the closed-auction problem the rewrite claims to avoid. This is the same objection critique 2 raised about rate-card states, and it is not answered.

In Texas, where open enrollment is real (HHSC takes FMSA applications year-round and contracts noncompetitively), entry is free. The qualification therefore needs no purchase. What a buyer pays 1x revenue for is a book of participants who can switch FMSA at will, plus the seller's referral relationships. The rewrite's own selling point, participant choice, is what makes the acquired asset non-sticky and key-person dependent. A fixed rate with free entry also means every funded entrant competes for the same margin, and Texas FMSA counts and profitability are not sized.

Rate cards are revocable and tied to budgets. Colorado applied a 1.6% across-the-board cut in Oct 2025 (the FMS PMPM was untouched that time). Texas sets its rate by biennial review. Critique 2 listed state cuts to self-direction in MD, MO, ID, IN and CO. The rewrite files policy risk as 'not fixable' and then concentrates the thesis in budget-authority, family-caregiver-heavy programs, which are the segment most exposed to the federal and state fraud and cut push.

The acquisition math contradicts itself. The plan buys at about 1.0x revenue and calls that 6x EBITDA, which implies sellers earn about 17% EBITDA. The median case then earns 5-8% EBITDA on about $25M revenue, or $1.3-2M. On roughly $24-26M invested (about $20M of acquired revenue at 1.0x, plus about $4M of reserves, plus bid costs), that is 12-20x EBITDA actually paid. An exit at 8-10x would return $10-20M on $25M, a capital loss. The 'median' case is effectively a bear case, and the real success probability is the 8-10% upside only. This is my arithmetic from the rewrite's own figures.

Even the upside is a mediocre financial outcome. $103M of revenue at a blended 10-12% EBITDA is about $10-12M. At the roughly 10x multiples the rewrite cites for TEAM and GT, that is $100-125M of enterprise value against $60-75M of equity and debt invested over about 7 years. That is roughly 1.4-2.1x, or about 5-11% IRR before fees and dilution (my arithmetic). Revenue of $100M is not the right success test for a roll-up.

The deal count and capital do not fit the pitch. The pitch says 'buy two or three' operators with 2-6k participants each. At $110-150 PMPM that is about $8-32M of revenue in total. The upside needs 43k participants in the choice and plan segments ($69M of revenue) and budgets $35-45M of acquired revenue. That implies 6-17 deals, or 25k+ participants of organic growth in referral-driven markets with unknown customer acquisition cost. The de novo CAC read is a side note and has no result. The count of non-sponsor operators of 2-6k participants with clean records is unknown and is probably small. The only small non-sponsor operators with public financials, three of the four in Wisconsin (iLife, Premier, Outreach), lose money, and the rewrite excludes them.

The two-week test cannot reliably resolve the riskiest assumption. Seller self-reports of margin are biased upward. Asking prices anchor high. 'Fewer than 5 of 25 will share numbers' is a likely outcome for cold calls from an unknown with no capital, and it would kill the idea on access rather than on truth. The plan also says a seasoned FMS co-founder is a precondition for owner-operator trust, but sequences that recruitment after the test. A pass (3 operators with cost at or under $90, 2 open to a sale at or under 1.0x) still would not show that a buy at scale works.

Several upside links remain unsupported. The roughly 6-10 statewide rebids in the window versus about one competitive award a year nationally is an unreconciled assumption. A first-time winner taking 2 of them against PPL, Tempus, Palco and GT is optimistic. Dropping statewide RFPs from the plan would remove $23.6M, but the plan keeps them because the qualification thesis needs them. Statewide pricing at $77-83 has only loss-making and +2% cost data behind it. The New York slice depends on a receivership or statute that is unconfirmed.

HHAX sits under the plan-delegated segment as prime vendor and can squeeze the fiscal agent to a subcontract fee (the rewrite admits this). The Acumen-TEAM link remains unconfirmed, so the sponsor-comp logic is shaky in both directions. The Wisconsin protest outcome is still unknown. No FMS deal price exists anywhere, so the entire entry thesis is a stipulated multiple. A seasoned co-founder and $60-75M of capital are preconditions that the founder does not have, so this is a search-fund or PE roll-up and not a startup.
riskiest_assumption: Small, non-sponsor-owned fiscal agents exist in choice and rate-card markets that earn at least 15-20% gross margin at $110+ per participant-month and will sell at a price their cash flow can carry (about 1.0x revenue, about 6x EBITDA, both assumptions). The qualification ticket, the ladder to statewide RFPs and the whole upside depend on buying that ticket cheaply. No FMS-only deal price has been found by me or by any critic.
two_week_test: Seller-side price and cost discovery, no capital. Days 1-2: list 25 owner-operated or nonprofit FMS operators from the Minnesota DHS FMS provider pages, Texas HHSC FMSA choice lists and MCO lists, and Colorado, Michigan and Virginia lists, excluding GT, Acumen/TEAM, PPL and Consumer Direct Care Network; pull Form 990s for the nonprofits. Days 2-12: contact all 25, aiming for 8-10 conversations plus 2 healthcare-services M&A advisers; ask six fixed questions (participants and states, revenue PMPM, cost PMPM, EBITDA margin, any payroll-tax or wage-hour claims, willingness to sell and the multiple they have been told). Days 12-14: apply thresholds written in advance. Pass: at least 3 operators show cost at or under $90 at $110+ revenue and at least 2 would consider a sale at or under 1.0x revenue. Kill (alive becomes false): median ask above 1.5x revenue, or reported margins under 5% at $110+, or fewer than 5 of 25 will share numbers. In between: shrink the premium assumption and rerun the cases. Second gate at month 6: a signed LOI at or under 1.0x revenue plus a committed equity partner, or stop.

judge_rationales.vc:
This is a decent-sounding small-cap services roll-up, not a seed-stage venture opportunity. A seed fund would pass on it, and a search fund or PE sponsor would be the right audience.

Size of prize: The whole US fee pool is roughly $0.7-0.9B. The pitch's own upside is $103M of revenue at a blended 10-12% EBITDA. That is about $10-12M of EBITDA and perhaps $100-125M of enterprise value at the ~10x multiples cited. It would take $60-75M of equity and debt over about 7 years. The second-round critic's arithmetic gives roughly 1.4-2.1x, which is far below venture return. The "median" case is $25M of revenue at 5-8% margin. At ~1x revenue purchase prices, that implies something like 12-20x EBITDA paid. In practice it is a bear case, so the real success case is an 8-10% joint event. Seed benchmarks like Stripe, Toast and Samsara had multi-billion outcomes with credible 100x paths. This has none.

Why now: The policy swing toward multi-vendor choice (the DOJ suit against New York's PPL award, Wisconsin audit scrutiny, Alabama and Minnesota multi-award) is real, as is commoditized FMS software (HHAX, Annkissam, DCI, CYMA). But sponsors (H.I.G. in GT Independence, General Atlantic in TEAM at ~10x) are already buying the same assets, which makes entry more expensive. Federal and state pressure on family-caregiver self-direction is the main demand-side risk. The open procurement windows (New York, West Virginia, Alabama, Ohio, Wisconsin) are mostly closed or locked. So timing is mixed: the political backlash helps the counter-positioning story, but the roll-up window is closing.

Non-consensus and right: The rewrite is honest and it conceded most of the early critiques. Its idea is to buy the qualification stack rather than build technology, and to enter through enrollment and rate-card markets. That is a thoughtful, non-obvious roll-up thesis, but the premise is shaky in specifics. Colorado is an RFP-awarded vendor list, not open enrollment. Minnesota's $165-250 fee is participant-paid and tiered down to $50-155 for small nonprofits. In Texas, where entry really is free, qualification needs no purchase, and an acquired book is switchable at will. Rate cards can be revoked by the state. So the "scarce asset" is partly free where it is open and closed where it is scarce.

Feasibility and defensibility: The riskiest assumption is unevidenced. No FMS-only deal price exists, and the only observable small non-sponsor operators (Wisconsin's) lose money. The deal count also does not fit, since 2-3 buys of 2-6k participants cannot reach 79k. The seasoned co-founder is a precondition that is sequenced after the test, the founder lacks the $60-75M, and the two-week test is biased by seller self-reporting and cold-call access. Defensibility is moderate at best: technology is explicitly not a moat, scale economies are unproven, and the contracts are revocable and annually renewable.

Evidence of demand: The spend is mandated and signed by a state, so the market exists. But there is no evidence of a willing seller at a workable price, no evidence that a premium-fee segment is large, and no evidence that anyone pays for reliability.

Net: a capable operator might build a $20-30M-revenue services business, which is a decent small business, but not venture-scale.
judge_rationales.operator:
This is a services roll-up, not a seed-stage company, and it scores as a decent-sounding but capital-heavy, thin-margin small-business thesis.

Demand and pain (4): The spend is real, mandated and state-signed, with about $0.7-0.9B a year in fees. But the demand is not for anything this company sells. States and plans don't have an urgent, unmet pain that a new fiscal agent solves. The customer is a seller-owner of an existing operator, and the dossier found no FMS-only deal price. The premium-fee segment ($140+) rests on mis-specified evidence. Minnesota's fee is participant-paid and tiered, with small nonprofits charging $50-155. Colorado is a closed five-year RFP list, not an enrollment market. Texas has free entry, so there is nothing to buy except a switchable book. The only public cost data (Wisconsin) shows small operators losing money. The first-10-customers test is just a single acquisition, which needs capital the founder doesn't have.

Unit economics and capital efficiency (very poor): The plan assumes a 5-8% EBITDA margin in the median case. It buys at about 1.0x revenue, so the effective multiple paid is roughly 12-20x EBITDA on the median case. That is a capital loss at the 8-10x exit multiples it cites. Even the $103M upside is about $10-12M EBITDA, or roughly 1.4-2.1x on $60-75M invested over about 7 years. For a founder who builds profitable companies, this has the wrong shape: heavy capital, low margin, long hold, and licenses that states can revoke.
